item.title: Wales grind out frustrating WXV win against Japan
item.description: Wales earn a three-try victory against Japan in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure a second win of their WXV campaign.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

WXV Global Series

Japan (0) 0

Wales (7) 17

Tries: Lockwood 2, K Jones Con: Bell

Wales ground out a win over Japan in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure their second victory of this WXV campaign.

Swirling wind, rain and humidity made for a real battle between sides ranked 11th and 12th in the world, with a scrappy first-half looking likely to end scoreless.

But scrum-half Seren Lockwood's 35th-minute snipe gave the game a much-needed spark and the visitors a 7-0 advantage at the break.

Wales lost centre Freya Bell to a serious-looking knee injury, but the impact of the bench proved the difference as Kelsey Jones drove over off a lineout ball, before Lockwood finished a rare moment of class at the death.

It was far from an impressive performance from Sean Lynn's resurgent Wales, but given their previous results, his side have now proven the ability to win ugly.

The two sides will meet again in Kumagaya City on Saturday, 31 October.

Centenary celebrations dampened

The hosts, who were playing in a double header with the men's side to celebrate Japanese rugby's centenary, had twice run Ireland close before their meeting with Wales.

But indiscipline has been somewhat of an Achilles heel, and they lost flanker Nami Asari to a yellow card just six minutes into the Test.

Wales looked to have taken immediate advantage from a five-metre driving lineout, with Jones peeling off to cross for what would have been her ninth international try, but on review, lock Jorja Aiono was deemed to have caused an obstruction.

Japan hit back with some attacking phases of their own, with Bell and Sisilia Tuipulotu combining well to hold prop Wako Kitano up over the line.

Wales continued to look comfortable in defence as Japan patiently went through the phases, but the visitors' renewed attacking prowess looked disjointed amid wayward kicks and handling errors.

It was disappointing, considering Wales' 74-point haul in their previous two outings against South Africa and USA, but then conditions were not in their favour.

The breakthrough eventually came five minutes before the break, and it was again off a driving lineout.

The powerful Bell trucked the ball up to the line, with Lockwood quick to the breakdown and quick to spot a gap in the defence.

Bell added the conversion to end the half.

Bell injury blow

Japan came back out with much more attacking intent and looked more threatening as Wales began to slip off tackles.

Lynn's side were also dealt a blow when a distraught-looking Bell was stretchered off the pitch with a serious-looking injury, but there was an able replacement waiting in Courtney Keight.

Lleucu George was also introduced before the hour mark as Wales looked to win back some territory, and the backline reshuffle paid off when they added a second try on a rare visit to Japan's 22 on 65 minutes.

And this time there was no denying Jones at the back of the driving maul, with Wales putting some breathing space between themselves and their hosts.

They looked to have added an immediate third try when Lockwood won the chase from Bevan's hack through, but replays showed Jones' turnover in the build-up had been from an offside position.

Lockwood did, however, bag her second three minutes from time, with the makeshift wing finishing well after George's floating pass out wide.

Wales pushed for a try bonus-point with Nami Yoshida sin-binned, but had to settle for three to go with a first clean sheet since beating Hong Kong 65-0 in November 2018.

How they lined up

Japan: Nishi; Tsunokawa, Langford, Kataoka, Nishimura; Tsukui (capt), Harada; Komaki, Nagaoka, Kitano, Kawamura, Sato, Asari, Korai, Bodman.

Replacements: Nagata, Yoshida, Fuji, Yoshimura, Jennifer, Seo, Ito, Havili Kagawa.

Sin bin: Asari (6 mins), Yoshida (76 mins)

Wales: Neumann; N Metcalfe, Cox, Bell, A Williams; Bevan, Lockwood; M Davies, K Jones, Tuipulotu, B Metcalfe, Aiono, K Williams (co-capt), Callender (co-capt), King.

Replacements: Reardon, Pyrs, E Jones, Crabb, G Evans, B Lewis, George, Keight.

Referee: Julianne Zussman (Canada).

Assistant referees: Sunny Lee (Hong Kong China) & Hibiki Ikeda (Japan).

TMO: Matt Rodden (Hong Kong China).

item.title: Ferguson's first game as Glentoran boss postponed
item.description: Duncan Ferguson's first game as Glentoran manager against Ballymena United is off because of a waterlogged pitch.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Duncan Ferguson's first game as Glentoran manager against Ballymena United has been postponed because of a waterlogged pitch.

The Glens were set to host the Sky Blues at the Oval on Saturday at 15:00 BST, but, after a pitch inspection at 12:00, the decision was taken to call the game off.

The Everton legend, who was confirmed as Glentoran boss on Monday, will now take charge of his new team for the first time away to Coleraine on Friday, 30 October at 19:45 GMT, live on BBC iPlayer.

A yellow Met Office weather warning is in place across Northern Ireland from 10:00 BST on Saturday until 12:00 GMT on Sunday.

There is also an amber weather warning in place for Saturday night with strong winds of up to 75mph expected.

Saturday's Women's Challenge Cup final between Glentoran and Cliftonville was also postponed on Friday because of the weather warning.

item.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
item.description: The full feasibility study will look in detail at how hosting the Games in northern England could work.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

A £7m fund to explore how the Olympics could be brought to northern England will be announced in John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, the BBC has learned.

The chancellor plans to allocate the money for a full feasibility study on the possibility for a bid for a "Northern Games".

If successful, it could see the games held in the North in the 2040s.

The last time the UK hosted the Olympics was London 2012. A UK Trade and Investment (UKTI) department report estimated in 2013 it boosted the economy by £9.9bn, although the amount was met with some scepticism.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC: "Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly.

"The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of.

"We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it."

In May the government asked UK Sport to carry out an initial assessment of the idea, looking at the possible cost and benefit of a bid to hold the Olympics across the North.

The idea had been put forward by Northern Mayors and backed by a group of former Olympians including Dame Laura Kenny and Dame Sarah Storey.

As part of next week's Budget the government will announce the next step - a "full feasibility study".

The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost £8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a £9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

The new feasability study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

item.title: Poor England suffer another Australia humiliation
item.description: England are well beaten by defending champions Australia in their second Women's Rugby League World Cup Group A match in Perth.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Australia (36) 78

Tries: Chapman 2, Kelleher 2, Church 2, Kelly 2, Robinson, Aiken, Kernick, Dodd, Weale, Penitani Gray, Bent Goals: Kelleher 9

England (0) 0

After talk of lessons learned and improvements made, reality struck fast for England. They conceded a penalty just one second into their match against Australia - as Lucy Murray was two yards offside from kick-off.

It set the tone for another humiliating defeat, one which shows the gap to the Jillaroos has not shrunk since the thrashing in Las Vegas in March 2025.

On that occasion, England were 38-0 down at the break before losing 90-4. In Perth, Australia led 36-0 at the interval before winning 78-0.

England were not expected to beat World Cup co-hosts and reigning champions Australia in Group A. The Jillaroos have lost one international since 2016.

It is quite another thing for England to be as passive and error-prone as they were in this game, limp in the tackle and with questionable body language. Only six of this England squad were in Las Vegas, but quality-wise little has changed.

After ceding advantage from the kick-off, England saw off the initial danger but were caught out chasing the kick from their try-line. Australia countered and Jaime Chapman scored.

England muffed the kick off for the second time in succession, straight out of play. Australia immediately attacked; after seven minutes, Chapman got up to take a high catch from Jocelyn Kelleher's kick and score.

After a brief flash where England thought they scored in the corner but Anna Davies' knee was in touch, they cheaply give the ball away and Tamika Upton broke two tackles before Kelleher crossed.

As Kelleher came round over the try-line to improve the position for the kick, wing Amelia Brown turned her back to play. It gave the impression England had already given up.

It was damage limitation for England, while the hosts could show off. After a score from Julia Robinson - who suffered a broken wrist shortly afterwards when being pinned by a team mate - Kelleher sliced in a swerving goal-kick of which Roberto Carlos would be proud.

Kelleher added her second try, and from the resulting kick off they attacked again, ending in Isabelle Kelly running over Fran Goldthorp.

Abbi Church crossed in the corner for 36-0. Soon after the restart, Australia went from one end to the other for Tarryn Aitken to bring up 40.

Olivia Kernick ran through three players in the non-existent defence to score, before Quincy Dodd forced over the 10th try under the posts.

Australia were in full showboat mode. Kelleher chip-kicked for herself before pinging an over-shoulder pass that led to Church's second try. The 12th try came as desperate England defence was not enough to stop Makenzie Weale.

The 13th came from Tiana Penitani Gray after a Brown knock-on, before Australia captain Kelly scored her second.

Shaylee Bent concluded the thumping, ending a move where multiple England tackles were shrugged off without blinking.

There was added pain for England as second row Eva Hunter exited with an ankle injury in the first half.

It adds to the loss of Jasmin Strange, who picked up a serious knee injury in training on Tuesday and was pitchside on crutches.

Goldthorp, England's best player on the night, carried on despite a nasty blow to her wrist.

As expected, England's qualification will come down to a decider against Samoa next Friday - where they must be better.

item.title: New British number one Boulter loses Japan semi-final
item.description: New British number one Katie Boulter loses 6-1 6-4 to Czech doubles specialist Katerina Siniakova in the Japan Open semi-finals.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Katie Boulter has lost in the Japan Open semi-finals, in her first match since reclaiming the British number one spot from Sonny Kartal.

Kartal moved above Boulter in the world rankings by reaching the final of last week's Wuhan Open.

But Boulter's run to the last four in Osaka, which included a victory over Antonia Ruzic in the quarter-finals, will be enough for her to go back above Kartal when the rankings are next updated.

However, the 30-year-old missed the chance to reach the final, and a shot at a fifth WTA singles title, losing 6-1 6-4 to doubles world number one Siniakova.

Eighth seed Boulter rallied after being swept aside in the opening set, going a break up at the start of the second.

But Siniakova, also 30, maintained her bid for a first singles title in four years by claiming two hard-fought breaks of her own to wrap up victory in 85 minutes.

She will now play 2023 champion Ashlyn Krueger in Sunday's final after the 22-year-old American beat compatriot and top seed Ann Li 6-4 6-7 (4-7) 6-3.

item.title: Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority'
item.description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino laughs off questions about whether he considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.

In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof".

"There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."

Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016.

The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".

Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.

Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.

He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).

Fifa has done some things 'maybe less good'

During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".

But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.

He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.

Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it".

"We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.

Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".

He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.

Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.

"I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.

"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."

He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.

England among teams at U15 World Cup

Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.

England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.

This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.

Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves.

"It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said.

"When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

item.title: Kompany recovery will take 'weeks' as tests continue
item.description: Vincent Kompany remains stable in hospital as doctors run tests following his collapse on Friday, says Bayern Munich director Max Eberl.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany needs "protecting from himself" and will take weeks to recover after collapsing at the club's training ground on Friday, said the club's director of sport Max Eberl.

Former Manchester City and Belgium defender Kompany, 40, remains in a "stable" condition in hospital and "examinations were continuing".

Eberl added that Bayern had considered asking for Sunday's Bundesliga game at Freiburg to be postponed, but believed the best tonic for Kompany would be to "play and be successful".

"Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We're not starting to put together any timeframes," said Eberl.

"We need to firstly figure out what it is and then we'll discuss calmly what the recovery time is to be. We won't be talking about days, but weeks. We need to all be clear on that."

Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train.

He had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday for Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.

Kompany was on the touchline for Wednesday's match and Eberl questioned whether he "should have put the brakes on him earlier".

"The fact is, we protect our coach wherever we can," he said.

"If a coach says he feels ready to do something, then we're not going to say 'we won't allow that' if we don't know what's going on.

"It's also everyone's own responsibility to say, 'I can't carry on now'.

"Vinnie's a hard worker. If you don't listen to the subtle signals your body sends, eventually it will scream out in pain.

"Vinnie will be given that time [now], and we'll continue to try, even more than before, to protect him from himself."

Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups, before going into management with Burnley.

After guiding them to the 2022-23 Championship title, Kompany was unable to keep the Clarets in the Premier League.

He left to take over at Bayern in May 2024 and has led them to successive Bundesliga titles.

Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has spoken with the Bayern boss in hospital.

"I explained to him that we would be having no football conversations," said Danks. "It was just checking in on his health and making sure he's OK.

"All the football operations are in our hands and we'll work together as a team to keep the club moving forward."

item.title: No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning
item.description: A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses, their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run ended, and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016 - England are not invincible.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Before England's three-match series against Canada, few would have predicted this outcome.

A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses; their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run – stretching back nearly four years – ended; and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016.

Over the past 13 months, Canada have turned a 33-13 defeat in the World Cup final into a statement 31-22 win in Ottawa. And three years out from the 2029 World Cup, they have laid down an early marker of their title credentials.

More than that, they have proved England are not invincible – a reality which should hearten New Zealand and perennial Women's Six Nations bridesmaids France because both have beaten giant-killers Canada in the past 12 months.

For the second time in eight days, England captain Meg Jones has been called upon to take stock of a defeat. Once again, she opted for a message of defiance.

"It was a hell of a contest. We're not broken, we just need to grow," said Jones. "Do it together, use the lessons. We're playing the best teams, getting the best punches thrown at us.

"I genuinely believe we've got the best players in the world. When we're firing, generally we're unstoppable. We don't dwell on the past, we're not anxious about the future, we're focused on the present."

It's true, this is far from panic stations. In 2016, England were the defending world champions when they lost to France and beaten finalists Canada. Since then, they've been imperious, winning a second World Cup, reaching the final in 2017 and 2022, and lifting nine of the past 10 Six Nations titles.

This is only their third defeat in 74 matches, so perspective is required.

But England's performances throughout the WXV Global Series highlighted areas for improvement.

They have lacked their usual clinical edge in attack. In Ottawa, Sarah Bern was held up over the line and England conceded a turnover less than five metres out as they failed to make their dominance pay before the break.

Tellingly, they opted to kick a penalty early in the second half to close the deficit – perhaps a lesson learned from last month's 26-26 draw in Exeter, where they turned down a shot at goal to snatch the win in the dying moments.

In defence, they have conceded 18 tries across their past five matches in the WXV, compared to eight in six at the World Cup. They have trailed at the break three times, something they hadn't experienced since 2020.

Last week, ill-discipline repeatedly gifted Canada field position before a late handling error, which put a clearing kick under pressure, opened the door for the hosts' winning try.

On Friday night, Gabrielle Senft picked off a bouncing ball from a missed pass to set up Canada's second try. Minutes later, England were lucky not to concede a similar try when a pass bisected Jess Breach and Jones, who pounced on the ball just before Lizzie Gibson got to it.

"We were riding the waves, building phases, scrum, set piece, we were very strong. Sometimes it's the bounce of the ball or it doesn't swing your way. We couldn't execute when we got in their 22, that's a big one to reflect on for sure," said Jones.

England 'will suffer' if young players don't get PWR game time

Canada does not have a professional women's domestic league and their players had to launch a crowd-funding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.

It's unsurprising, therefore, that many of Canada's top talents play domestically in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, which offers a level of training and match experience they cannot find elsewhere.

Twenty-five Canadian players are contracted for the 2026-27 season, with 11 featuring in July's PWR final between Saracens and Trailfinders. Three Canadian coaches, including head coach Kevin Rouet at Saracens, are also involved in English domestic rugby.

PWR squads must have a minimum of 13 England qualified players in a matchday squad.

But England head coach John Mitchell has warned that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides.

"I think it's necessary to make sure that young English girls are getting enough PWR time," Mitchell said. "It's a critical pathway because Sevens is definitely gone. For players aged between 19 and 23, it's critical.

"We're just going to make sure we don't erode our depth as a result of [overseas involvement]. It's not so much about now. It will be the future that will suffer if we're not smart in that area."

Mitchell has been forced to call upon England's squad depth on multiple occasions in 2026 with Abby Dow and Emily Scarratt retiring after the World Cup, four players absent through pregnancy, and several big names – including Hannah Botterman, Alex Matthews, and Amy Cokayne – spending time on the sidelines because of injury.

He's handed out more than half a dozen debuts this year, with hooker Bryony Field particularly impressing during September's home internationals, played the likes of Abi Burton and Ellie Kildunne out of position, and brought Liz Crake back into the fold after several years away.

item.title: Wall on South Africa, surfing and pink scrum caps
item.description: Ahead of Ireland's WXV Tests in South Africa, Dorothy Wall discusses the Springboks, surfing and her iconic pink scrum cap.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

When Dorothy Wall steps on to a rugby pitch, she stands out.

Wall and her distinctive pink scrum cap will be in action on Saturday in Cape Town when Ireland take on South Africa [14:30 BST] in the first of two Tests in the WXV Global Series.

But why did she pick up the eye-catching headwear?

She admits she is often asked the question, even if the answer is somewhat simple - she doesn't want cauliflower ears.

"When we played Australia in 2024, I got a really bad cauliflower ear," said the Ireland second row.

"Probably the worst pain I've ever felt, it was the worst thing ever. Way worse than my Achilles and I also don't want cauliflowers for my future.

"So that's when I had to get a scrum cap and I was like, 'oh if I'm doing it, I may as well just go pink'. That was it really."

Ireland have vastly improved under head coach Scott Bemand, but their WXV campaign has had a mixed start.

They were beaten by the USA in their opener but bounced back with a win over Japan in Galway.

Ireland then defeated Japan for a second game in a Test outside the WXV.

South Africa have also had a mixed start as wins over Spain and Italy were followed by a heavy defeat by Wales.

Ireland are playing in South Africa for the first time and are aiming to mark the occasion with a historic win.

For Wall and Ireland, it is not just about winning but in the manner that they do it.

"We're very much process-driven, so results on any given day, it kind of comes back to the process of what we're trying to do.

"I think we're looking for wins, but more gratifying wins, in a way, that we aren't leaking tries in defence, or taking opportunities when they come.

"Maul definitely was a big focus for us, and just taking opportunities and finishing those opportunities."

Wall notes the physicality of the South Africans, and says their scrum is "incredibly dominant".

Despite that, she believes "our set piece and our line-out are better".

"Our kicking game, especially with Dannah [O'Brien], is very influential on how we play, and I think we're a very fit team," she said.

"Those attributes will definitely be used to hopefully beat the South Africans in the next two games."

Exeter move has added 'diversity' to game

After coming through the set-up in Ireland and playing for Munster domestically, Wall made the move to England in 2024 to sign for Exeter Chiefs.

She had been in the Sevens programme before moving into 15s for her Ireland debut in the 2020 Six Nations.

Wall had just graduated from University College Dublin when she made the move to Exeter, and said that "change can be a really positive thing".

"I'd been professionally contracted either with Sevens or fifteens since I was 18.

"It was one of those things that came up as a life decision as well, seeing a different part of the world, even if it's not that far away.

"It was just an opportunity that I wanted to take to play with other internationals.

"We have a lot of New Zealanders, Canadians, Red Roses, and with every international you come across, you learn something different from them."

Wall also noted that it has added "diversity" in her rugby experience, and playing for Ireland is another level of intensity.

"As much as I love Exeter, I equally, if not more, love playing for Ireland.

"Both have kind of married well over the last two years."

One of the perks of living in Exeter is the proximity to the Cornish coastline, but it's fair to say that surfing is not one of her past times.

"You know what, I am incredibly bad at anything that isn't rugby, including surfing or skating or anything like that.

"My mum came over last summer after the Six Nations and we did St. Ives and all around the coast there.

"It was when we had the heat wave so it felt like we were in France. It was really nice to actually see the area, which we enjoyed a lot."

item.title: England thrash France to keep alive World Cup hopes
item.description: England beat France 82-0 to maintain their hopes of reaching the Men's Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

England (36) 82

Tries: Farnworth 3, Young 3, Lewis 2, Ashton, Williams, Radley, Litten, Welsby, Brimson Goals: Savala 13

France (0) 0

After losing their opener, then watching Tonga and Samoa rack up huge victories, England knew only a massive win over France in Perth would keep alive their World Cup dreams.

Mission accomplished: 82-0. But they still require a lot of work and a pinch of luck to reach the semi-finals.

England needed this margin of victory following their 30-12 defeat by Tonga last Saturday

They must do the same against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday - then hope Tonga beat Samoa next Sunday.

After a nervy opening quarter, in which England looked weighed down by expectations and permutations, they finally got going with three tries in four first-half minutes.

By half-time, England had six converted tries on the board including a Herbie Farnworth hat-trick. Come full time, Dom Young also bagged a treble and England had 14.

After 23 minutes, England found their breakthrough as captain George Williams - overwhelmed by Tonga last week and initially nervy here - broke the line before a clever behind-the-back pass set up Young to score in the corner.

England had, belatedly, arrived at this World Cup as a force to be reckoned with. Soon after, full-back AJ Brimson - whose direct runs pierced France time and again - led a breakaway before finding Matty Ashton.

The wing had knocked on over the try line early on to spill a seemingly certain England opener, but made no mistake here for his seventh try in six Tests.

Harry Smith spotted the gap before setting up Farnworth for his first try on 27 minutes. And after a period of defence against a France side - who threatened sporadically but made too many simple mistakes - Farnworth scored again nine minutes later.

Williams powered over under the posts for 30-0, and then came England's best move of the World Cup just before the break - slick through the hands to the right before Young set Farnworth back in for his third.

Eight minutes after the break, Young chased down a grubber kick to bring up 40 points - before Jez Litten and Williams cut through a tiring defence and Victor Radley scored unopposed.

England needed to repel another French siege, before overpowering at the other end for Litten - who impressed as an interchange - to score. Another Brimson surge led the way for try number 10, scored by Mikey Lewis.

A dreadful short kick-off was caught by Young, who raced through for his hat-trick. Jack Welsby got on the act for try 12, a third score in four minutes, as the French surrendered.

The 13th try - scored by Lewis who broke through two weak tackles - ensured England surpassed Samoa's 74-point winning margin against the French.

After a frustrating few minutes where they had to defend deep for their clean sheet, England finally reached 80 as Brimson scored a deserved try.

Hugo Savala was also a key figure with superb kicking. He only missed one goal from 14 attempts, adding 26 points.

England are far from perfect. They made six errors in the opening 20 minutes - and a better side than France, who haven't reached the semi-finals since 1992, would have taken advantage.

But it all comes down to points on the scoreboard - and England must hope they have enough.

After Samoa thrashed Papua New Guinea 62-6 earlier, England were a massive 150 behind the Samoans on points difference - which, if Tonga beat Samoa next weekend, would be the deciding factor between the teams as to who reaches the semis.

A hefty win here helps the English cause, but they still need work and luck to avoid missing the World Cup last four for the first time ever.

item.title: Latte Lath's journey from street games and Carrick to new start in Germany
item.description: Emmanuel Latte Lath's journey took him from Ivory Coast to Italy as a child, now he is making another new start in Germany.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Emmanuel Latte Lath remembers the feeling he experienced as an eight-year-old when his journey from Ivory Coast, his country of birth, to a new life in Italy began.

"I started to realise when I was on the plane and I saw people different than me, I was a bit scared," the ex-Middlesbrough striker tells BBC Sport.

The Ivorian forward, now playing for Union Berlin, was six years old when he discovered he was moving to Europe, finally making the move two years later.

Despite leaving behind many friends and family in the west African country, he would be reunited with his father in Italy, which gave him an opportunity to grow their relationship.

"It was important because when I was born, it wasn't that close," the 27-year-old says.

"He went to Italy to find a better life, so it wasn't that easy talking with him every time by phone. I was missing this part from my father.

"When I saw him, it was kind of a new life, new motivation to stay close to my father, and then everything started again. It looks like I had two lives."

This reconnection with his father helped him settle into his different surroundings, although he still missed parts of the life he had as a young child in Africa, especially the freedom he found playing football.

Latte Lath explains: "Me and my five friends, we just built our team and we would go to play against another city, there was like no pressure, nothing.

"It was just funny moments, enjoying football there, and it was quite competitive because it was almost every time finishing in some fights, so it was street rules. I was one of the most competitive.

"I missed it. Always together, being with my friends. It was really, really fun."

Those early football experiences were extremely important for Latte Lath when he arrived in Italy, settling into his new life and attempting to learn the language.

Before he arrived he would never play in boots, and had never been part of an official team, but that quickly changed once in Europe.

"It was exciting to learn and to show my potential," says the Union Berlin striker.

"It was difficult in the beginning because I didn't know the language, but I had a really good person who helped me.

"It was important for me because I didn't have too many friends there. But I was just there to play football and after go home, I know timing will come."

He continued to develop and joined Atalanta's prestigious academy in 2015. Two years later he was scoring against Juventus in his third appearance for La Dea in the Coppa Italia.

"It's unbelievable, it's unforgettable. The emotion I had there, it's still the same when I'm thinking about it now," he says.

"The week before I was home with my family, we were just laughing and they were saying, 'imagine if I go, imagine,' and one week after that it happened."

That would be the only goal he scored for the club and it would be the last time he wore the shirt competitively.

Instead he would embark on a nomadic five-year journey on loan to eight clubs, a path many young footballers growing up in Italy face as they struggle to break into the top flight.

"I think Italian football has always been one of the difficult football environments because it's a lot of tactics, a lot of rules also," he says.

"So it doesn't let you express yourself because you have to play with too many or a lot of rules.

"So it was difficult also to make a step, but it was also difficult to maybe keep going with the steps I made, but this gave me power to make a different choice."

'Carrick a good coach and person'

It was after a prolific loan spell with Swiss club St. Gallen that a move to Middlesbrough in the Championship materialised.

When Latte Lath arrived in the north east of England in 2023, he met Michael Carrick, the head coach at the time, who helped the Ivorian settle and become one of the best strikers in England's second tier.

"I found a good coach and a good person. It gave me straight away confidence," he says.

"He was a calm person, a calm coach, maybe sometimes too much, but it was needed for us. He knew always when and what he should say to you in the difficult moment or in the good moment.

"So for me, I think in that point of my life, it was really important."

That confidence Carrick instilled in him helped Latte Lath score 29 goals in 67 games and earn a move to Major League Soccer side Atlanta United as the most expensive signing in the league's history at the time.

But his time in America did not live up to the expectations and in the summer he moved back to Europe on loan to Union Berlin, where he has got to experience the unique culture of the city and Die Eisernen.

He continues: "I arrived here and I am surprised because the fans' passion is crazy. This is something new for me. It gives me an extra muscle, another power to do well.

"Berlin is huge, I love different cultures, and you can find different cultures and people. I think I can fit in because I grew up with different friends and cultures."

item.title: Fastest pitch in World Series history as Brewers win opener
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in the opening game of the best-of-seven World Series as both sides aim for their first title.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Milwaukee Brewers starting pitcher Jacob Misiorowski threw the fastest recorded pitch in World Series history as his side began the best-of-seven season finale with a win.

The right-hander played a starring role in the 3-2 win at home to the Tampa Bay Rays, in the first match of the 122nd World Series.

It is only the second time in more than a century that neither side contesting the World Series has won the title before.

A sell-out crowd watched the Brewers in only their second appearance in the finale of the Major League Baseball season, and their first since losing to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982.

Milwaukee's American Family Field has 41,900 seats but with standing-room-only tickets available for the 'Fall Classic', 43,250 fans packed in to see the game.

"It was amazing - just to have the city behind me, it means the world, we couldn't ask for anything better," said Misiorowski.

The Brewers host the second match of the best-of-seven series on Saturday before the teams move to Florida for three games, then return to Milwaukee for the final two matches, if needed.

Misiorowski, 24, became the youngest starter since 1997 to win a World Series opener, after restricting the Rays to just one run in five innings.

His fastest pitch at 103.5 mph beat the previous mark of 103.2 mph set by Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs in 2016 - though speeds have only been recorded since 2008.

Brewers designated hitter Christian Yelich also played a key role, scoring one run and driving in another as they took a 3-1 lead.

The Rays added one run in the final inning and had a runner on third base as they pushed to level the score, but Milwaukee closed out victory.

"It feels great. The guys settled in right away and did a great job," Yelich said. "We've still got a ways to go but nice to get that first one."

The Brewers made the World Series by beating the Los Angeles Dodgers 4-0 to claim the National League title, while the Rays clinched the American League pennant with a 4-2 win over the Cleveland Guardians to reach the post-season finale for only the third time.

The Rays lost to the Philadelphia Phillies in the 2008 World Series and the Dodgers in 2020, but manager Kevin Cash took solace from the fact that they tested the Brewers on Friday.

"We came up a little bit short, but there's some benefit maybe from a loss," said Cash.

item.title: Wales great Faletau suffers fresh injury blow
item.description: Wales number eight Taulupe Faletau suffers another injury blow after just one game back with Cardiff.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Wales number eight Taulupe Faletau has been sidelined again after injuring a finger on his Cardiff comeback.

The 35-year-old made his first appearance since March in the Champions Cup defeat by Northampton on 18 October.

He made an accomplished return but reported pain in a finger in the days afterwards and will have surgery.

Faletau will miss the United Rugby Championship (URC) derby at Ospreys that finishes the first block of the season.

It is hoped he will be fit to return after the November break for the Nations Championship.

"Unfortunately he had a little bit of a niggle with a pinkie finger, so he will be on the sidelines for a while," said Cardiff head coach Corniel van Zyl.

"He will miss the Ospreys game but hopefully after November he will be fine."

Faletau has played only 31 times for Cardiff since joining from Bath in 2022 and was limited to seven appearances last season because of shoulder, calf and knee injuries.

"I can imagine he is quite frustrated because after the game he didn't even realise it, then the next day it was sore all of a sudden," said Van Zyl.

"It's a tough one for him to take, but hopefully he can turn it around."

Faletau's lack of game-time meant he was not included in Wales' squad for the Nations Championship, with in-form Cardiff team-mate Taine Basham getting a recall instead.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy said they would not rule out an international return for Faletau, who has won 109 caps and played at three World Cups, but that he needed to show durability to go along with his undoubted quality.

The latest blow only adds to those fears about the legendary number eight, who signed a one-year contract extension with Cardiff last summer.

Cardiff will not only be without Faletau against Ospreys on Saturday, 31 October but their Wales back-row forwards Alex Mann, James Botham and Basham.

They will hope that number eight Alun Lawrence, who has not featured this season because of a number of niggles, will be fit for the trip to Swansea.

Dan Thomas, summer signing Semisi Paea and youngster Lucas de la Rua have played in the back row this season, with hooker Evan Lloyd another option.

Cardiff suffered a third successive loss when beaten by Sharks at the Arms Park on Friday.

item.title: Volkanovski nears featherweight immortality as record beckons
item.description: Alexander Volkanovski will stake his claim to be the greatest featherweight of all time if he beats Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Alexander Volkanovski is already widely regarded as one of the best featherweights of all time, but is he about to become the greatest?

The Australian will defend his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi on Saturday as he seeks to add another accolade to an already glittering career.

Now in his second championship run, the 38-year-old will earn a record ninth win in UFC featherweight title fights if he triumphs against the Russian.

Victory would allow Volkanovski to surpass Brazilian icon Jose Aldo, whom many regard as the best featherweight of all time.

Fans and pundits have hotly debated the topic of the greatest featherweight, with American Max Holloway also considered among the best, but the modest Volkanovski refuses to engage with it.

"I think a lot of fighters don't like answering these questions, I'll leave everyone else to make these decisions," said Volkanovski.

"I'm not fussed about belts, title defences, numbers and all that. When I say I don't care - it is cool, but that's not what drives me.

"I'm not driven by getting the most title wins. I get more drive for the challenges and getting through those challenges."

When Volkanovski lost his featherweight title after being knocked out by Ilia Topuria in 2024, many thought his career was coming to an end.

The defeat was his third in four fights and second straight knockout after losing to Islam Makhachev only four months prior when attempting to win the lightweight belt.

Volkanovski has said he likes to return to action as soon as possible after defeat to right the wrong, but this time he took 14 months off.

Volkanovski was booked against Diego Lopes upon his return last year, with many believing retirement beckoned in the face of one of the UFC's brightest prospects.

But the Australian put on a masterclass to regain his belt, before repeating the performance in February to cement his place as the promotion's featherweight king.

To Volkanovski, overcoming adversity in what many regard as the twilight of his career means much more than breaking records.

"The things I'm doing at this age and how I'm doing it, is the real depth," said Volkanovski.

"When people throw out 'he's old' - I'm loving that. I want people thinking I'm too old and declining because when I overcome and get through, it's like 'how's he still doing it?' I'll play into that 100%."

History books lean towards Volkanovski

Volkanovski is not a knockout artist or submission specialist, and he does not overwhelm opponents with his wrestling.

What he is, is one of the most well-rounded mixed martial artists in history.

Volkanovski's footwork, distance management, boxing and cardio are world class, which has helped him dominate opponents such as Holloway and Lopes.

When it comes to grappling, Volkanovski has gritty takedown and submission defence, which helped him compete gamely in the first fight against Makhachev and overcome the odds against Brian Ortega in 2021.

At 18 minutes and three seconds, Volkanovski has the longest average fight time in UFC featherweight history, illustrating his mastery inside the octagon.

His 11-fight UFC winning streak between 2016 and 2023 is second to Holloway's record 13, while his 1,623 significant strikes total is also bettered by the American's remarkable 2,971.

What Volkanovski holds over Holloway, however, is three victories, while he also beat Aldo in 2019.

Volkanovski might not want to admit it, but the stats and history books are weighing heavier than ever in his favour as the greatest featherweight of all time.

In 32-year-old Evloev, Volkanovski faces another difficult challenge with the Russian undefeated in 20 bouts and on a 10-fight winning streak in the UFC.

Win or lose, Volkanovski says he is not considering retiring, but added a "super fight" against lightweight champion Justin Gaethje could convince him to hang up his gloves.

Volkanovski has twice failed to become a two-division champion, with both defeats coming against Makhachev.

The first loss in 2023 was razor thin, with some believing Volkanovski should have been awarded victory with the Australian pushing the Russian harder over five rounds than any other opponent.

After reclaiming his throne at featherweight, winning a belt in a second division is one of the few things which Volkanovski is yet to tick off in the UFC.

"If I can fit in the equation of the lightweight division - we know Justin is unsure of what he wants to do next," said Volkanovski.

"I don't have any plans of retiring other than if we were to do something like this then maybe it's a super-fight, champion versus champion and we see ourselves off.

"It's something I would retire for, otherwise I'm taking each fight as it goes."

item.title: Smith v Puello world title fight predictions
item.description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's light-welterweight title fight between WBC champion Dalton Smith and Alberto Puello.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Dalton Smith will make the first defence of his WBC light-welterweight title on home soil when he faces former champion Alberto Puello in Sheffield on Saturday.

Unbeaten Smith, 29, returns to the ring for the first time since becoming world champion with a stunning knockout of Subriel Matias in New York in January.

Dominican Republic fighter Puello, 32, is aiming to become a three-time world champion, having lost his WBC belt to Matias on points last year.

Smith will have the backing of his home crowd at the Utilita Arena. Can he keep his dream of fighting at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough stadium alive with another win?

Or will the tricky and experienced southpaw Puello, who has lost just once in 26 professional fights, ruin the homecoming?

BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions on who will come out on top.

Chantelle Cameron - two-weight world champion

"I think it's going to be a great fight, I think there will be a lot of close rounds, but I'm going for a majority decision win for Smith in a really tough fight."

Prediction - Smith

Darren Barker - former middleweight world champion

"What a brilliant fight this is. It's such a terrific match-up with contrasting styles. You have a slick southpaw in Puello and the tough, rugged, well-schooled Smith. Puello being a southpaw will suit Dalton who throws a fantastic right hand.

"This is fine margins - high-level chess. I think Dalton will come through via decision, or perhaps a late stoppage, and he will have produced two back-to-back victories to cement his place in the top 15 pound-for-pound rankings."

Prediction - Smith

Carl Frampton - former two-weight world champion

"I think this will be an interesting fight. Both guys have a similar sort of style. Puello is a boxer-puncher who goes really well to the body. He throws that loopy left hand shot quite well that Dalton will have to be quite careful of.

"It will be cagey at the start and I think Puello will fall behind a little bit. Dalton is a better boxer than him and better at his game. Puello will then have to come forward and I think that will suit Dalton.

"So I see Dalton winning quite a wide points decision."

Prediction - Smith

Denzel Bentley - WBO middleweight champion

"It's a good fight and I think Puello is a good fighter but I'm Team Smith. He boxes well and his style has matured. Puello has fast hands and is good in close but Smith can find a way to beat him. If he knocks him out then it's a big statement, but I'll go for a Smith win on points."

Prediction - Smith

Barry Jones - former super-featherweight world champion

"This is a harder fight for Smith than Matias. Matias was a monster, while Puello is a clever boxer who sits on the back foot and punches nice and long. He's southpaw which makes it awkward to adjust your feet and stance.

"Ultimately, I think the angles of attack will be the difference for Smith. I think it might be a bit of a frustrating night for him but I think he comes out on top on points.

"It will be relatively entertaining - not as exciting as the win over Matias, perhaps - but a good homecoming for the champion."

Prediction - Smith

Viddal Riley - European cruiserweight world champion

"I'm backing Dalton, he's been my guy since we were 12 years old. He was my roomate at every tournament and now is his time as WBC world champion."

Prediction - Smith

Lee Selby - former featherweight world champion

"I'm backing Dalton Smith to beat Alberto Puello and retain his world title. Smith's power, accuracy and impressive stoppage win over Subriel Matias make him a dangerous opponent.

"Although Puello's experience and awkward southpaw style could make it a tough fight, I think Smith's power and work-rate will prove too much. Smith to win by unanimous decision."

Prediction - Smith

Paulie Malignaggi - former two-weight world champion

"Puello can be awkward and disrupt rhythm as he did in wins over guys like now WBA champion Gary Antuanne Russell, but Dalton's a big light-welterweight and his boxing is on point as well as intelligent decision-making.

"His stoppage win over Subriel Matias was impressive but I see Dalton winning this one on points. Puello will complicate things in some moments, but Smith wins a comfortable decision."

Prediction - Smith

Ade Oladipo - DAZN presenter

"It's a big fight. I think the Utilita Arena - pound-for-pound - is the noisiest venue in the country. To use a football analogy, I think it will have to be a 12th man for Dalton.

"I think he's up against it. Puello is a very special talent, as is Dalton who put on a performance of a lifetime in January.

"Dalton has a lot of the advantages but Puello comes here with experience at the highest level at this division. He wants the belt back, which he thinks was robbed from him in his loss to Matias.

"I do edge towards the current champion because of home advantage, but I wouldn't be shocked if Puello walks away with the belt."

Prediction - Smith

Adam Smith - DAZN commentator

"Dalton is a real hero in Sheffield but Puello is very dangerous. He's a southpaw and a former two-time world champion.

"It's a very tough first defence but Dalton has home advantage, the age and the unbeaten record. He probably has plans A, B, C and D. He's a very clever boxer whose background has been perfect - an excellent amateur and a solid professional."

"I expect him to come through a very tough test."

Prediction - Smith

Zelfa Barrett - British lightweight

"I think Dalton will stop him late on - round nine or 10. Dalton is just too good for Puello, he'll try to put pressure on but Dalton will just have his number."

Prediction - Smith

Richie Woodhall - former super-middleweight world champion

"Dalton will have a little bit too much speed and a little bit too much flair. The one thing that Dalton has to watch out for is he cannot afford to slow it down to Puello's pace. He's decent with his jab, he likes his opponent to stand in front, he doesn't like it when they move.

"If Dalton is in and out with his feet, plays it tricky, he'll be able to beat him fairly comfortably as long as he doesn't stand and trade."

Prediction - Smith

Harlem Eubank - British welterweight

"I've got Dalton winning on points. I think it will be a competitive fight but Dalton will edge it."

Prediction - Smith
